did_you_know.text: The chapter opens with the command addressed to both Moses and Aaron. This fits laws that concern both everyday life and the priestly system of ritual purity.
A camel does chew its cud, but its foot is not a split hoof like that of cattle or sheep; it has two toes resting on a broad pad.
The biblical word shafan is sometimes translated as “rabbit,” but many identify it with the rock hyrax, an animal that lives among the rocky hills of the Middle East.
The identity of the animal called arnevet is also not completely certain. Ancient animal names do not always match the scientific names used today.
The pig meets one of the dietary signs: it has a split hoof. But it lacks the second sign, chewing the cud.
The Torah uses two visible signs for identifying water creatures: fins and scales. This is a practical classification based on observation, not a modern scientific taxonomy.
Many of the bird names in this chapter cannot be identified with certainty today. As a result, different translations may give different names for the same bird.
The bat appears in the list of “birds,” even though it is a mammal in modern biology. Here, “bird” refers to a flying creature, not to a modern biological category.
Locusts and grasshoppers have been eaten for centuries in parts of the Middle East and North Africa. The chapter permits only certain kinds, and the exact identity of some names is uncertain.
The impurity caused by touching an animal carcass lasts until evening, so it is temporary rather than permanent. This is an important pattern in the chapter’s purity laws.
The chapter distinguishes between touching a carcass and carrying it: the person who carries it must also wash his clothes. This highlights the greater involvement of carrying.
Earthenware absorbs liquids through its walls, so it cannot be cleaned in the same way as metal or stone. That is why the Torah commands that a clay vessel contaminated from within be broken.
The chapter distinguishes between dry seed and seed that has become wet: water makes the seed subject to impurity. This is a ritual rule, not a modern explanation of how germs spread.

A spring and a water reservoir remain pure even if a carcass falls into them, but a person who touches the carcass becomes impure. The verse distinguishes the water source from the person who contacts the impurity.
The word nefesh here does not mean only “soul” in the modern sense; it often refers to the person or to life itself. The warning therefore concerns the whole person.
The chapter presents the dietary laws as part of a call to holiness, not merely as rules of health or hygiene. The stated reason is to be holy, in relation to God’s holiness.
